concept.name: Key rate duration
concept.definition: A measure of a bond's or portfolio's price sensitivity to a change in yield at one specific maturity point on the curve, holding other points fixed. The set of key rate durations across maturities decomposes total interest-rate sensitivity, and they sum (approximately) to the effective duration.
concept.intuition: Instead of asking 'what if all rates move?', it asks 'what if only the 5-year rate moves?' — locating where along the curve a portfolio's risk actually sits.
concept.mechanics: The yield at a chosen key maturity (e.g. 2, 5, 10, 30 years) is shifted by a small amount (with the shift tapered to neighboring points), the security is repriced both ways, and duration is computed from the price changes; repeating across 11 standard maturities gives a sensitivity profile used for non-parallel curve hedging.
concept.formula: KRD_i = (P(−) − P(+)) / (2 × Δy × P_0), where P(−), P(+) are prices after a 1% down/up shift of the key rate at maturity i, and P_0 the original price.
concept.failure_modes: Real yield curves rarely move one point at a time, so isolated key rate shifts are artificial; results also depend on how the shift is tapered to adjacent maturities, making values convention-dependent.
concept.misconceptions: A high total duration does not reveal curve exposure: two portfolios with the same effective duration can have very different key rate profiles and behave oppositely when the curve twists.
concept.example: A portfolio with a 10-year key rate duration of 4.0 loses roughly 4% of value if the 10-year rate alone rises 100 bp, regardless of what other maturities do.
